verses.zh: 不可严责老年人，只要劝他如同父亲；劝少年人如同弟兄；
verses.en: Do not address an older man harshly[NOTE:1] but appeal to him as a father. Speak to younger men as brothers,[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “Do not speak harshly to an older man.”
No verb “speak” is stated in this clause, but it continues the sense of the preceding.
verses.commentary:
5:1 "Do not sharply rebuke" This is an AORIST ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE with the
NEGATIVE PARTICLE, which usually means do not start an act. This is a strong Greek
term (used only here), which literally means "to strike blows" (cf. 1 Tim. 3:13). Christians must act
differently, they must always act in love with a view toward reconciliation. This advice may reflect the
OT admonition to honor the aged in Lev. 19:32.

▣ "an older man" This is literally the term "elder" (presbuteros). There are two
senses in which this term is used in this context:

- for an older man (1 Tim. 5:1)

- for a leadership position in the local house churches (1 Tim. 5:17 cf. 1 Pet. 5:1,5)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELDER

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN AGING

▣ "but rather appeal to him as a father" This is a
PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE. Paul's emphasis is for Timothy to treat the members
of the house churches as his closest family members (cf. Mark 3:31-35). The honor and respect due
"fathers and mothers" may reflect the Ten Commandments (cf. Exod. 20:12 and note 1 Tim. 5:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HONOR FATHER AND MOTHER

verses.zh: 劝老年妇女如同母亲；劝少年妇女如同姊妹；总要清清洁洁的。
verses.en: older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters—with complete purity.
verses.commentary:
5:2 "younger women as sisters, in all purity" Because of (1) Timothy's age and (2) the sexual
exploitation of the false teachers (cf. 2 Tim. 3:6), Paul was especially careful to emphasize purity in
relation to the young women.

verses.zh: 要尊敬那真为寡妇的。
verses.en: Honor[NOTE:1] widows who are truly in need.[NOTE:2]
notes: The word honor here carries the double meaning of respect and financial support. This Greek word can imply both senses, and both are intended in this context.
Grk “the real widows,” “those who are really widows.”
verses.commentary:
5:3-16 Are these permanent guidelines for all churches in all cultures through time? The Bible records

- things it does not advocate

- things for a limited time and culture

How do modern Bible believers know the difference? This is a great question with no clear answers.

- check all Scripture

- use common sense

- allow some freedom on peripheral issues

Two of my favorite commentators have addressed this issue.

- Gordon Fee, Gospel and Spirit

- F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 116-117

5:3 "Honor widows" The term "honor" in 1 Tim. 5:3 and 17 may denote a salary or a stipend
the church gave

- to needy widows (cf. 1 Tim. 5:3-8)

- to special women helpers (cf. 1 Tim. 5:9-16)

- to the elders (cf. 1 Tim. 5:17-22)

It seems that the church, following the OT and synagogue (cf. Deut. 24:17-22;
Exod. 22:22-24; Isa. 1:17; Acts 6:1ff; 9:39,41), cared for widows. It was Paul's concern that those the
church helped were really in need or had no family of their own to help them (cf. 1 Tim. 5:4,16). The
false teachers exploited widows (cf. 1 Tim. 5:6,15). Paul admonishes the church to help true widows.

verses.en: But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to fulfill their duty[NOTE:1] toward their own household and so repay their parents what is owed them.[NOTE:2] For this is what pleases God.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “to practice their religion.”
Or “and so make some repayment to their parents”; Grk “and to give back recompense to their parents.”
Grk “for this is pleasing in the sight of God.”
verses.commentary:
5:4 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE (as is 1 Tim. 5:8).
There were widows who were being neglected by their own families (cf. 1 Tim. 5:8,16).

▣ "practice piety" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: GODLINESS

▣ "for this is acceptable in the sight of God" This probably refers to the Ten
Commandments about honoring father and mother (cf. Exod. 20:12), in this case a widowed
mother. In the OT God defends the weak, socially disenfranchised, and powerless. The cry
to defend "the widow, the orphan, and the alien" becomes as characteristic here as the
Deuteronomic phrase (repeated in Jeremiah).

Believers show their love and respect for YHWH by honoring His word and
will for maintaining strong family ties and responsibilities.

verses.zh: 那独居无靠、真为寡妇的，是仰赖　神，昼夜不住地祈求祷告。
verses.en: But the widow who is truly in need, and completely on her own,[NOTE:1] has set her hope on God and continues in her pleas and prayers night and day.
notes: Or “left all alone.”
verses.commentary:
5:5 "Now she who is a widow indeed and who has been left alone" This is the same
rare grammatical construction as 1 Tim. 4:3 (i.e., an ADJECTIVE and a PARTICIPLE,
cf. Titus 1:15). One wonders if this was a literary marker of a scribe who Paul used in the Pastoral
Letters. Paul gives specific guidelines for his day on the qualification for receiving help from the
church (but not on the "list" of 1 Tim. 5:9):

- PERFECT TENSE ‒ has and continues to live alone

- PERFECT TENSE ‒ has been and continues to be a godly woman

- PERFECT TENSE ‒ continues to flee earthly pleasures by means of continual prayer

Anna (Luke 2:37) and Dorcas (Acts 9:36) (although she is not specifically said
to be a widow), would fit these qualifications.

notes: For “is dead even” the Greek text reads “has died.”

5:6

NASB
"But she who gives herself to wanton pleasure"

NKJV
"but she who lives in pleasure"

NRSV
"who lives for pleasure"

TEV

Because of the cultural situation this may refer to

This seems to be a very stern warning (cf. 1 Tim. 5:15).

This same word is used in James 5:5.

▣ "is dead even while she lives" This refers to a state of spiritual death
(PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE). This verse is describing widows in the
house churches of Ephesus! The false teachers had brought about not only their own spiritual
"deaths," but now they are spiritually responsible for the "deaths" of others.

verses.en: Reinforce[NOTE:1] these commands,[NOTE:2] so that they will be beyond reproach.
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “and command these things.”
verses.commentary:
5:7

NASB
"Prescribe these things"

NKJV
"these things command"

NRSV
"give these commands"

TEV
"give them these instructions"

NJB
"instruct them in this"

Peshitta

This term refers to "strict military commands" (cf. 1 Tim. 1:3,18; 4:11).
These were not suggestions! These were not items of personal preference.

▣ "so that they may be above reproach" The "they" seems to refer to the
relatives of widows with living families (cf. v. 8). This was and is an appropriate calling for all
believers. Whoever fails to provide for his own relatives, especially his immediate family,
has disowned the faith and in the eyes of the community is worse than an unbeliever
(1 Tim. 5:7,8). This reflects Jesus' teachings in Mark 7:9-13. This seems to relate to the
continual emphasis on giving no handle for criticism, both to believers and unbelievers
(cf. 1 Tim. 3:2,7,10; 5:7; 6:14). Christians must always live so as to attract others to faith in
Christ. The positive side of this is seen in verse 4, while this is the negative.

verses.zh: 人若不看顾亲属，就是背了真道，比不信的人还不好，不看顾自己家里的人，更是如此。
verses.en: But if someone does not provide for his own,[NOTE:1] especially his own family, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
notes: That is, “his own relatives.”
verses.commentary:
5:8 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE meaning

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII

▣ "denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" I believe this refers to
the person's witness in the community (cf. 1 Tim. 5:7; 3:4-5), not to their salvation (see Hard Sayings
of the Bible, pp. 671-673). Even unbelievers help their own families. However, there are other texts
which use this same term "deny" and imply a total rejection of God (cf. 2 Tim. 2:12; Titus 1:16; 2 Pet. 2:1;
Jude 4). In context this may somehow be related to the actions or teachings of the false teachers "who fell
away from the faith" (cf. 1 Tim. 1:19-20; 4:1-2; 6:9-10,20-21) or their followers (cf. 1 Tim. 5:6,15).

verses.zh: 寡妇记在册子上，必须年纪到六十岁，从来只作一个丈夫的妻子，
verses.en: No widow should be put on the list[NOTE:1] unless[NOTE:2] she is at least sixty years old, was the wife of one husband,[NOTE:3]
notes: This list was an official enrollment, apparently with a formal pledge to continue as a widow and serve the Lord in that way (cf. v. 12). It was either (1) the list of “true widows” who were given support by the church or (2) a smaller group of older women among the supported widows who were qualified for special service (perhaps to orphans, other widows, the sick, etc.). Most commentators understand it to be the former, since a special group is not indicated clearly. See G. W. Knight, Pastoral Epistles, 222-23 for discussion.
Grk “let a widow be enrolled if she has reached not less than sixty years.”
Or “a woman married only once,” “was devoted solely to her husband” (see the note on “wife” in 1 Tim 3:2; also 1 Tim 3:12; Titus 1:6).
verses.commentary:
5:9 "A widow is to be put on the list only if she is not less than sixty years old" This is
a PRESENT PASSIVE IMPERATIVE with the NEGATIVE PARTICLE,
which usually implies stop an act in process. Here is another qualification for the widows who
were part of the ministry team.

The term "the list" is the Greek term for "a legal register." The
widows' roll may be synonymous with the concept of "deaconess" (cf. 1 Tim. 3:11; Rom. 16:1).
However, the "Apostolic Constitutions," written in the early second century, listed three
categories of women ministers: virgins, deaconesses, and widows.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEACONESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEMALE CHURCH WORKERS, III.

▣

NASB
"having been the wife of one man"

NKJV
"and not unless she has been the wife of one man"

NRSV
"and has been married only once"

TEV
"In addition she must have been married only once"

NJB
"who has had only one husband"

Peshitta
"who has been the wife of one man only"

There has been much discussion as to what this phrase means
(see full note at 1 Tim. 3:1,12). But it is obvious that whatever it means, it was a very
serious issue to the house churches of Ephesus and Crete (cf. 1 Tim. 3:1,12; 5:9;
Titus 1:6). Strong, godly families were (and are) a powerful witness to a lost and confused world.

For a more complete discussion see 1 Tim. 3:2. In 1 Tim. 5:14 young widows
are admonished to remarry. This seems to imply that a second marriage was not seen as
sinful (cf. Rom. 7:2-3; 1 Cor. 7). In Baptist circles in Europe this "husband of one wife"
or "wife of one man" has been interpreted as a biblical rejection of second marriages,
especially for pastors. However, this was not the case in middle eastern culture. This theory
reflects the growing asceticism of the early church, but not of the NT. Greek thought
(i.e., the body is evil) negatively impacted the early Gentile churches.

verses.zh: 又有行善的名声，就如养育儿女，接待远人，洗圣徒的脚，救济遭难的人，竭力行各样善事。
verses.en: and has a reputation for good works: as one who has raised children,[NOTE:1] practiced hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, helped those in distress—as one who has exhibited all kinds of good works.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “if she raised children.” The phrase “if she raised children” begins a series of conditional clauses running to the end of the verse. These provide specific examples of her good works (v. 10a).
Grk “followed after every good work.”
verses.commentary:
5:10 "having a reputation for good works" There are five specific good deeds listed
(all FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCES) in the remainder of 1 Tim. 5:10.
These good works reflect a woman's expected role in the local community.

SPECIAL TOPIC: QUALIFICATIONS FOR FEMALE CHURCH WORKERS

▣ "if" This is a series of five FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCES
in 1 Tim. 5:10, each of which denotes a qualification of a widow to be hired by the church.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII

▣ "if she has brought up children" This is not meant to imply that a childless
woman cannot be considered, but that if she has had children, they must be godly. This is
the recurrent emphasis (cf. chapter 3) upon a strong, godly, faithful family life.

▣ "if she has shown hospitality to strangers" This does not refer to the welcoming
of any and everybody into one's home, but the boarding of itinerant Christian leaders.

▣ "if she has washed the saints' feet" This was an act of a household servant
receiving a guest. Jesus did this for His own disciples to teach them humility (cf. John 13). Here
it seems to be imagery of humble service (and possibly a culturally expected hospitality).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SAINTS

▣ "if she has assisted those in distress" Here again this probably refers to a
comforting ministry toward believers, but it could include needy, hurting, lost neighbors. Each
of the qualifications reveals the servant heart of these elder widows.

verses.zh: 至于年轻的寡妇，就可以辞她；因为她们的情欲发动，违背基督的时候就想要嫁人。
verses.en: But do not accept younger widows on the list,[NOTE:1] because their passions may lead them away from Christ[NOTE:2] and they will desire to marry,
notes: Grk “refuse younger widows.”
With a single verb and object, this clause means “pursue sensuous desires in opposition to Christ.”
verses.commentary:
5:11 "But refuse to put younger widows on the list for when they feel
sensual desires in disregard of Christ, they want to get married" We must remember the
positive theology of marriage which is presented in the Bible (cf. Genesis 1 and 2). This
phrase seems to relate to a vow that these widows took when they became house church
helpers (cf. 1 Tim. 5:12). This is not a disparaging statement about marriage, but a disparaging
comment about

- making a vow in Christ's name and not keeping it (i.e., as divorce does also)

- possibly marrying outside the faith (cf. v. 12; NASB Study Bible, p. 1766)

The Greek term pistis, which is usually translated "faith,"

verses.zh: 并且她们又习惯懒惰，挨家闲游；不但是懒惰，又说长道短，好管闲事，说些不当说的话。
verses.en: And besides that, going around[NOTE:1] from house to house they learn to be lazy,[NOTE:2] and they are not only lazy, but also gossips and busybodies, talking about things they should not.[NOTE:3]
notes: L&N 15.23 suggests the meaning, “to move about from place to place, with significant changes in direction—‘to travel about, to wander about.’”

Or “idle.” The whole clause (“going around from house to house, they learn to be lazy”) reverses the order of the Greek. The present participle περιερχόμεναι (perierchomenai) may be taken as temporal (“while going around”), instrumental (“by going around”) or result (“with the result that they go around”).
Grk “saying the things that are unnecessary.” Or perhaps “talking about things that are none of their business.”
verses.commentary:
5:13 "as they go around from house to house" Possibly the widows helped in daily
care and weekly distribution of food (as did the synagogue) to the members of all the different
house churches. They may have visited house to house to check on believers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

▣ "gossips and busybodies" The first term is used in 3 John 10 of false charges
being brought against a church leader. The problem is clearly defined in Titus 1:11. The problem
was not idle gossip, but promoting heresy!

The second term is used of magic or sorcery in Acts 19:19. However, in this
context it applies to women who make their business tending to other people's business
(NJB "meddlers").

▣ "talking about things not proper to mention" In the context of the
Pastoral Letters the false teachers were tricking young women (cf. 2 Tim. 3:5-7).

It is possible that they were spreading the false teachings from house
church to house church or from Christian homemaker to Christian homemaker (cf. Titus 1:11).
This is why Paul will not let them speak publicly in the house churches (cf. 1 Tim. 2:9-15)
and will not allow them to be church helpers (i.e., younger widows).

calling (cf. 1 Tim. 2:15).

▣ "give the enemy no occasion for reproach" The "enemy" is
SINGULAR; it could refer to

- Satan (cf. 1 Tim. 5:15)

- anti-Christian pagan neighbors (NJB footnote, Jerome Biblical Commentary, p. 356)

- a false teacher (cf. 2 Tim. 3:6-7)

These widows who had become sexually active have opened a door for
both satanic attack and criticism from the whole community (believing and unbelieving).

The term "occasion" is a military term for a "beachhead" or "base of
operations" (cf. Rom. 7:8,11). The physical body is not evil, but it is the battleground of
temptation. Human sexuality is not the problem. It is fallen humans taking God-given
good things beyond God-given bounds.

wants Christian families to care for (PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE) their own

verses.zh: 那善于管理教会的长老，当以为配受加倍的敬奉；那劳苦传道教导人的，更当如此。
verses.en: Elders who provide effective leadership[NOTE:1] must be counted worthy[NOTE:2] of double honor,[NOTE:3] especially those who work hard in speaking[NOTE:4] and teaching.
notes: Grk “who lead well.”
Or “deserving.”
Like the similar use of “honor” in v. 3, this phrase denotes both respect and remuneration: “honor plus honorarium.”
Or “in preaching”; Grk “in word.”
verses.commentary:
5:17 "elders" The term "elder" (presbuteros) was an OT designation of
tribal leadership, while the term "overseer" (episkopos, cf. 1 Tim. 3:1) was a Greek
city-state designation of leadership. These two terms are used synonymously in the NT
(cf. Acts 20:17, 28 and 1 Pet. 5:1-2, where elder is used of pastors and also Titus 1:5,7,
where elder and overseer are used of the same leader).

The NT cannot be used to establish a divine church polity. It records
all three developed forms (i.e., Acts 15).

- episcopalian (James as authoritative leader)

- presbyterian (a group of elders reviewed)

- congregational (the congregations voted)

The PLURAL here and in Acts 20:17 and Titus 1:5
could possibly point toward house churches. The early church did not have separate
buildings until the third century A.D. No one home was large enough to accommodate all
the believers, therefore, different Christian homes around the larger cities opened
their doors for the regular meetings of the Christian community (usually divided by social status, wealth,
or ethnic issues). This approach also protected the church from being arrested all at once.

Exactly how the leadership of a city with several house churches
was organized is unclear (compare 1 Cor. 11:5 with 14:34). As the church grew, organization was needed. The form of
that organization is not as crucial as the godliness of the leaders.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BISHOPS/OVERSEERS

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH POLITY

▣ "worthy of double honor" This is a PRESENT PASSIVE IMPERATIVE.
It can refer to

- salary (cf. Gal. 6:6)

- esteem (cf. 1 Thess. 5:12-13)

- The following context of 1 Tim. 5:18 suggests salary.

See F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, p. 117.

▣ "especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching" Elders are
always mentioned in the PLURAL in the NT, which seems to imply
several local house churches in the larger cities like Ephesus (cf. Acts 20:17ff). Pastors
were to be able to teach as well as preach (cf. 1 Tim. 3:2; 2 Tim. 2:24; Eph. 4:11),
especially in areas affected by false teachers.

Some leaders have one spiritual gift and others another. Leaders must
focus on their giftedness and allow other gifted Christians to pick up the slack. Some
believers are wonderfully gifted for leadership, often in several ways. Those who function
in several areas need to be rewarded for their efforts and protected by the church in their
areas of ineffectiveness. We as the body of Christ rejoice in the giftedness of our members,
but we also need to remember that we desperately need one another (cf. 1 Cor. 12:7)!

5:18 "For the Scripture says" This is a quote from Deut. 25:4 (see notes online). It is
also quoted in 1 Cor. 9:6-7,14. The uniqueness of 1 Tim. 5:18 is that the OT is quoted on the
same standing as a NT quote that we find codified in Luke 10:7 ("the laborer is worthy of his
wages"). This shows Paul's view not only of the inspiration of the OT, but of the equality of
the emerging NT (also note how Peter does this same thing to Paul's writings, cf. 2 Pet. 3:15-16).

Paul's affirming the concept of a paid leadership is very interesting.

- Following his Jewish heritage, he did not usually take money from those he
taught (Philippi and Thessalonika were the exceptions).

- This very issue had been used by false teachers to attack Paul (as in Corinth cf. 2 Cor. 11:7-9; 12:13).

- There is probably some connection with this brief statement and the teaching of the false teachers,
but exactly what is not stated.

verses.zh: 控告长老的呈子，非有两三个见证就不要收。
verses.en: Do not accept an accusation against an elder unless it can be confirmed by two or three witnesses.[NOTE:1]
notes: An allusion to Deut 17:6; 19:15.
verses.commentary:
5:19 "Do not receive an accusation against an elder except on the basis of two or
three witnesses" This is PRESENT MIDDLE IMPERATIVE with the
NEGATIVE PARTICLE, which usually means "stop an act in process." This
reflects the turmoil and accusations caused by the false teachers.

The concept itself is from the writings of Moses (cf. Num. 35:30;
Deut. 17:6; 19:15, see notes online).

verses.zh: 犯罪的人，当在众人面前责备他，叫其余的人也可以惧怕。
verses.en: Those guilty of sin[NOTE:1] must be rebuked[NOTE:2] before all,[NOTE:3] as a warning to the rest.[NOTE:4]
notes: As a continuation of v. 19, this refers to elders who sin, not to sinning believers more generally.
Or “censured.” The Greek word implies exposing someone’s sin in order to bring correction.
“Before all” probably refers to the whole congregation, not just all the elders; “the rest” is more likely to denote the remaining elders.
Grk “that the rest may have fear.”
verses.commentary:
5:20 "Those who continue in sin" Notice the PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE.
In context this refers to leaders (i.e., Elders) who continue to sin (cf. 1 Cor. 3:10-15). This is not necessarily
a one-time act. Paul addresses the proper procedures for dealing with sinning believers in
Rom. 16:17-18; 1 Cor. 5; Gal. 6:1-5; 1 Thess. 5:14; 2 Thess. 3:6-15; 1 Tim. 1:20; 5:19-20; and
Titus 3:10-11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH DISCIPLINE

▣ "rebuke in the presence of all, so that the rest also will be fearful of sinning"
"Rebuke" is a common term in the Pastoral Letters (cf. 2 Tim. 4:2; Titus 1:9,13; 2:15). This seems
to speak of public (i.e., before the other elders or before the entire church) disciplinary
actions (cf. Gal. 2:14; James 5:16) which some elders took against others who had

- overstepped their authority

- promoted false teaching

- engaged in other inappropriate actions

The term "rest" may refer to

- the other house churches

- the other local elders

- other believers

verses.zh: 我在　神和基督耶稣并蒙拣选的天使面前嘱咐你：要遵守这些话，不可存成见，行事也不可有偏心。
verses.en: Before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels, I solemnly charge you to carry out these commands without prejudice or favoritism of any kind.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “doing nothing according to partiality.”
verses.commentary:
5:21 "I solemnly charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of His
chosen angels" This strong oath is found several times in the Pastoral Letters
(cf. 1 Tim. 5:21; 6:13; 2 Tim. 4:1; and in a related sense in 2 Tim. 2:14). Paul was serious
about the authority and origin of his teachings.

▣ "His chosen angels" It is somewhat surprising that "chosen angels"
are mentioned instead of the Holy Spirit. This is used in the sense of

- those who minister (i.e., "chosen messengers") to God's chosen people and who are present with them
(cf. Ps. 138:1; 1 Cor. 4:9; Matt. 18:10; Luke 9:26; and Heb. 1:14)

- those special angels near God's throne who are uniquely associated with His presence
(i.e., the Seraphim; in rabbinical literature, the seven angels of the presence)

- possibly "angel" is to be understood as "minister" and refers to other church leaders

This phrase is in direct contrast to Satan (cf. 1 Tim. 5:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERAPHIM

▣ "to maintain these principles without bias, doing nothing in a
spirit of partiality" Timothy is to have no favorites nor hold any grudges! The
term "maintain" is the Greek word for "guard."

- as God guards us (cf. 2 Thess. 3:2; Jude 1:24) and our inheritance (cf. 1 Pet. 1:4-5)

- we are to guard His truth

- We must also guard ourselves against false teaching (cf. 2 Tim. 4:15; 2 Pet. 3:17; 1 John 5:21).

Notice the covenant reciprocity: God keeps/guards us; believers must
keep/guard His truth and themselves (cf. Phil. 2:12-13)! It is possible that this charge to Timothy is related
to the favoritism and partiality shown by the false teachers claiming

- to be an elite group

- to have special knowledge

- special freedoms

verses.zh: 给人行按手的礼，不可急促；不要在别人的罪上有分，要保守自己清洁。
verses.en: Do not lay hands on anyone[NOTE:1] hastily and so identify with the sins of others.[NOTE:2] Keep yourself pure.
notes: In context “laying hands on anyone” refers to ordination or official installation of someone as an elder.
Grk “and do not share in the sins of others.”
verses.commentary:
5:22 "Do not lay hands upon anyone too hastily" This verse has three more
PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVES. It has been interpreted in two ways:

- to refer to ordination (cf. 1 Tim. 3:10; 4:14)

- to refer to accepting and reinstating a repentant elder who has been publically
reproved (cf. 1 Tim. 5:20)

Number 2 seems to fit the context of verses 24 and 25 and the historical
context of false teachers best.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAYING ON OF HANDS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ORDINATION

▣ "share responsibility for the sins of others" This may refer to

- ordaining too quickly (cf. 1 Tim. 3:6)

- restoring elders to leadership too quickly

Remember, the context is the activities of the false teachers infiltrating
the churches. Our actions can be interpreted by some as affirmation or approval of the
errors of others (cf. 2 John 11).

▣ "keep yourself free from sin" This is literally "keep yourself pure"
(PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE, cf. 1 Tim. 4:12; 5:2). Sin is

- an attitude

- an act

- an association

verses.zh: 因你胃口不清，屡次患病，再不要照常喝水，可以稍微用点酒。
verses.en: (Stop drinking just water, but use a little wine for your digestion[NOTE:1] and your frequent illnesses.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “for the sake of your stomach.”
This verse gives parenthetical advice to Timothy, to clarify what it means to keep pure (5:22c). Verse 24 resumes the instructions about elders.
verses.commentary:
5:23 "No longer drink water exclusively" This seems to be a parenthetical
comment to Timothy (NET Bible, p. 2182, #14). This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE
with a MĒ PARTICLE, which usually means to stop an act in process. Paul
is imploring Timothy to change his normal daily activity. The command "keep yourself pure" in
1 Tim. 5:22 is not affected by wine drinking! Be careful of denominational traditions that often
go beyond Scripture!

Timothy was apparently totally abstaining from wine. Paul mentions that wine
in non-intoxicating amounts should not be a problem for a church leader. We must remember that
the early Mediterranean world drank wine daily. This could mean (1) add a little fermented wine
to purify your water or (2) drink a little wine from time to time when your stomach acts up. Wine
is not the problem; fallen mankind's "misuse and abuse" is the problem. The Bible rails against
drunkenness (cf. Prov. 23:29-35; Isa. 5:11,22; 28:1-8), but does not teach total abstinence
(cf. 1 Tim. 3:3,8). In our day and society total abstinence by believers must be related to the spiritual concepts
found in Rom. 14:1-15:13; 1 Corinthians 8 and 10:23-33). However, believers must resist all forms
of asceticism (cf. Col. 2:20-23)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments" Are these two
different descriptive phrases or are they referring to one problem? Does this verse imply
Timothy was a physically weak person? Timothy's work was challenging and difficult. If he
was also physically weak, it makes him all the more a wonderful role model and noble person.

verses.zh: 有些人的罪是明显的，如同先到审判案前；有些人的罪是随后跟了去的。
verses.en: The sins of some people are obvious, going before them into judgment, but for others, they show up later.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “they [the sins] follow after others.”
verses.commentary:
5:24-25 These verses may relate to the warning in 1 Tim. 5:22. By their fruits ye shall
eventually know them (cf. Matt. 7:15-23). In context Paul addresses false teachers and true teachers.
They are evident by their teachings and lifestyles (sins that are evident) and other sins (i.e.,
hidden sins or attitudes/motives) will be revealed on Judgment Day.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- In light of the larger historical setting of the book, these words of pastoral advice
are probably also colored by the false teachers' actions

- problems with widows (1 Tim. 5:3-16)

- problems with elders (1 Tim. 5:17-25)

- problems with slaves (1 Tim. 6:1-2a)

- problems with false teachers (1 Tim. 6:2b-10)

- doctrine

- wealth

- There are three terms used in this section in two differing senses

- "elder"

- older man (1 Tim. 5:1)

- house church leader (1 Tim. 5:17)

- "widow"

- female survivor of a marriage that the church helped (1 Tim. 5:3-8)

- special category of female church worker that the church hired (i.e., "the widow's role," 1 Tim. 5:9-16)

- "honor"

- respect (1 Tim. 5:3, 17)

- salary (1 Tim. 5:3, 17)

- or both

- In some ways chapter 5 relates to chapter 3. The "elders" of 1 Tim. 5:17 refer to the
"overseers" of 1 Tim. 3:1 and the widow's "list" (roll) of 1 Tim. 5:9 refers to the "women"
of 1 Tim. 3:11.

I realize that this distinction between widows the church helped (1 Tim. 5:3-8)
and widows who served the church seems a bit of a stretch, but here is why I hold this view.

- The qualifications of a widow are strict (cf. 1 Tim. 5:5,9-10). Does this imply that the
church only helped some very special widows?

- The "roll" of 1 Tim. 5:9 seems to be a special list of widows.

- The "list" (cf. 1 Tim. 5:9) or the pledge (literally "the first faith") in 1 Tim. 5:12 implies
more than just a promise not to remarry. Why would remarrying be a problem? It would
remove the widow from needed church support, but what if it were a contract for church
employment? In this way the church helped needy persons (i.e., salary) yet also got
their services (i.e., serving other women).

- The discussion of "elders," which starts at 1 Tim. 5:17, involves church paid help. But, remember
these house churches were served by bi-vocational believers.
